c.tagline: Sulawesi's seafront gateway of sunsets, spice-trade forts, and grilled fish.

taxi.fareNote: Blue Bird is the reliable metered-taxi brand; insist on the meter, or use Gojek/Grab for fixed up-front fares. App-booked motorbike taxis (ojek) are cheapest for short hops through traffic.

emergency.note: 112 is the nationwide emergency line; 113 reaches the fire service.

avoid.reason: Bag-snatching and pickpocketing can occur along Losari Boardwalk and in minibuses (pete-pete) after dark.

hood_desc: Makassar's iconic seafront promenade and the city's social heart, lined with hotels, the floating mosques, and street stalls selling pisang epe at sunset; the most convenient and lively base for first-timers.
The historic colonial core around the 17th-century Dutch Fort Rotterdam and the La Galigo Museum, with old harbor streets and Chinatown nearby; best for history and sightseeing.
A modern commercial and business district built around Mall Panakkukang and the MTC, with shopping centers, chain hotels, and restaurants; a practical base away from the seafront.
A reclaimed seaside development south of the center with Akkarena Beach, the Trans Studio Makassar theme park, and GTC mall; a calmer, family-friendly resort-style area.
The gold-and-souvenir shopping street of Jalan Somba Opu beside the old Chinatown (Pecinan) around Jalan Sulawesi, famous for seafood restaurants and evening dining; lively after dark.
lodging: Novotel Makassar Grand Shayla City Center

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: Pete-pete and Trans Mamminasata BRT buses run roughly 6:00 AM to around 9-10:00 PM; after that, app-based ride-hailing and becak fill the gap.
transit.note: Makassar has no rail or metro. Getting around relies on pete-pete (shared minibuses, called angkot elsewhere), the Trans Mamminasata bus rapid transit (BRT) launched in 2014, becak (cycle rickshaws) for short trips, and app-based Gojek/Grab motorbike and car rides.
transit.pay: Pete-pete and becak fares are paid in cash to the driver and are cheap (a few thousand rupiah); negotiate becak fares before boarding. The Trans Mamminasata BRT charges a low flat fare paid on board.

bus: Intercity buses to Pare-Pare, Bulukumba (for Bira), and Tana Toraja from Daya and Malengkeri terminals
ferry: Pelni ships and inter-island boats from Soekarno-Hatta Port (Makassar) to Surabaya, Kalimantan, and eastern Indonesia
train: Maros section of the new Makassar-Parepare railway, South Sulawesi's first rail line, opening in phases

transit.m: Damri airport bus to the city center (~45-60 min)
Trans Mamminasata BRT connection toward the city
Airport taxi to Losari / city center (30-45 min)

tip.r: Not expected; some restaurants add a service charge, and rounding up the bill for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Coto Makassar
food.desc: Beef and offal simmered for hours in a cloudy broth thickened with ground peanuts and rice water, eaten with ketupat or coconut-rice burasa.

places.name: Coto Nusantara
places.note: One of the city's most famous coto houses, packed from breakfast onwards.

places.name: Coto Gagak
places.note: Long-running local favourite known for a rich, well-balanced broth.

places.name: Coto Maros Harimau
places.note: Legendary coto restaurant serving the Maros style since 1974.

food.name: Konro and Konro Bakar
food.desc: Beef ribs in a near-black soup of coriander and kluwak nut, or pulled from the broth, grilled and painted with peanut sauce as konro bakar.

places.name: Konro Karebosi
places.note: Open since 1968 on a family recipe; the benchmark for grilled konro.

places.name: Sop Konro Bawakaraeng
places.note: Legendary Makassar rib house trading since 1960.

places.name: Coto Nusantara
places.note: Handy if you want coto and konro in the same sitting.

food.name: Pallubasa
food.desc: Coto's richer cousin - beef and offal in a coconut-and-toasted-coconut broth, traditionally cracked with a raw egg yolk stirred into the bowl.

places.name: Pallubasa Serigala
places.note: The name everyone gives for pallubasa; queues form well before noon.

places.name: Pallubasa Onta
places.note: Long-standing rival serving the same dish in a more relaxed setting.

places.name: Coto Gagak
places.note: Serves pallubasa alongside its coto for an easy comparison.

food.name: Sop Saudara
food.desc: Clear, aromatic beef soup with rice vermicelli, fried potato patty and offal, served with grilled milkfish and sambal on the side.

places.name: Sop Saudara H. Dollahi
places.note: The best-known sop saudara house in the city, a fixture for decades.

places.name: Sop Konro Bawakaraeng
places.note: Serves sop saudara alongside its famous konro.

places.name: Karebosi area warungs
places.note: Cluster of soup houses near the central field, all serving the local classics.

food.name: Mie Titi
food.desc: Crisp deep-fried egg noodles buried under a thick, glossy gravy of chicken, prawn, squid and liver - a Makassar invention now copied nationwide.

places.name: Mie Titi
places.note: The original Makassar noodle house that gave the dish its name.

places.name: Mie Titi branches
places.note: Several outlets around the city if the original is full at dinner.

places.name: Karebosi area warungs
places.note: Nearby noodle stalls do their own versions of the crispy-noodle dish.

food.name: Pisang Epe
food.desc: Half-ripe kepok bananas grilled, pressed flat on the griddle and drenched in palm-sugar syrup, now also with cheese, chocolate or durian.

places.name: Pantai Losari pisang epe carts
places.note: Dozens of griddle carts line the seafront every evening - the classic Makassar sunset snack.

places.name: Anjungan Losari
places.note: Food stalls at the promenade platforms grill epe until late at night.

places.name: Jalan Somba Opu night stalls
places.note: Old-town street with evening snack vendors including pisang epe.

food.name: Sarabba
food.desc: Hot ginger drink boiled with palm sugar, coconut milk and pepper, often with an egg yolk beaten in - the Bugis-Makassar warm-up. Non-alcoholic.

places.name: Sarabba stalls, Jalan Sungai Cerekang
places.note: Street known for late-night sarabba stalls serving it with fried banana.

places.name: Pantai Losari food stalls
places.note: Seafront vendors pour sarabba alongside the pisang epe griddles.

places.name: Karebosi area warungs
places.note: Simple warungs keep a sarabba pot going through the evening.

food.name: Es Pisang Ijo
food.desc: Banana wrapped in green pandan crepe, served with sweet rice porridge, shaved ice and rose syrup - Makassar's iconic cooler. Non-alcoholic.

places.name: Pantai Losari dessert stalls
places.note: Pisang ijo and es palu butung sold from carts all along the seafront.

places.name: Es Pisang Ijo Bravo
places.note: Well-known dedicated pisang ijo shop with consistent quality.

places.name: Jalan Somba Opu night stalls
places.note: Evening vendors serve pisang ijo alongside other iced desserts.

landmarks: Fort Rotterdam (Benteng Rotterdam)
A remarkably preserved 17th-century Dutch colonial fort shaped like a sea turtle, the city's most iconic historic landmark.
Losari Beach
Makassar's famous waterfront promenade, beloved for its vivid sunsets over the Makassar Strait and lively evening food stalls.
Paotere Harbor
A bustling traditional harbor where majestic wooden Bugis pinisi schooners still dock, offering a glimpse of centuries-old maritime tradition.
99 Domes Mosque (Masjid 99 Kubah Al-Amirul Mukminin)
A striking waterfront mosque with 99 honeycomb-like domes symbolizing the names of Allah, a modern architectural marvel at Center Point of Indonesia.
Trans Studio Makassar
One of the world's largest indoor theme parks, an unmistakable landmark and popular attraction on the city skyline.
Somba Opu Fort
The reconstructed royal fort of the former Gowa Sultanate, showcasing traditional Makassarese architecture and cannons overlooking the strait.
Makassar Great Mosque (Masjid Raya Makassar)
The city's oldest and largest grand mosque, a historic and spiritual centerpiece of downtown Makassar.
Center Point of Indonesia (CPI)
A sprawling reclaimed waterfront district with promenades and monuments, envisioned as Makassar's modern civic showpiece.
Pantai Akkarena
A scenic recreational beach park popular for its palm-lined shore, sunset views, and family-friendly atmosphere.
La Galigo Museum
Housed within Fort Rotterdam, this museum showcases South Sulawesi's rich Bugis-Makassar cultural heritage and artifacts.

train.note: No international trains. Sulawesi's first railway, the Makassar-Parepare line, has begun limited operation on its northern section but does not yet serve central Makassar usefully - check current status before relying on it. For now almost all travel on Sulawesi is by road, sea or air.

bus.note: No international coaches. Terminal Daya north of the city has buses and shared Kijang minibuses north to Tana Toraja (about 8-9 hours) and on toward Palu and Manado; Bintang Prima and Litha & Co are the main operators. Book through redBus Indonesia (https://www.redbus.id/) or at the terminal.

intl.to: Java, Kalimantan, Papua & eastern Indonesia - sails from Soekarno-Hatta port

intl.op: ASDP and local boat operators — tickets at the harbour

ferry.note: No international sailings, but Makassar is the great crossroads of Indonesia's eastern shipping routes - Pelni ships call here on almost every long-distance line, heading for Surabaya, Balikpapan, Bau-Bau, Ambon and Papua. Voyages take days and deck class is very cheap. The port is close to the Losari waterfront. Book Pelni ahead around the Idul Fitri exodus.

half.name: Bantimurung Waterfall & Butterfly Park
half.blurb: A waterfall and karst reserve about 45 kilometers from Makassar known for its butterfly population and a limestone cave with prehistoric formations.

half.name: Malino
half.blurb: A cool hill town about 70 kilometers from Makassar with pine forests, waterfalls, and tea plantations at higher elevation than the coast.

half.name: Rammang-Rammang
half.blurb: A karst village north of Makassar surrounded by limestone towers, reached by boat through a river gorge lined with cliffs.
